finding: Properties 4 and 5 were both rewritten this round to form a partition over `--role <name>`, and the partition does not cover the emitted set. §4.2 defines the match set as "what this invocation would emit with `--role` removed" and names its own example: "`--perspective testing` emits `test-planner`, which is in neither" the corpus nor the built-ins. §4.2.1 defines the exit-2 case as a name "absent from the corpus for either phase, from `skipped_roles`, and from the built-ins" — three sources that do not include the emitted set. Measured on the current binary: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective testing --test-path internal` emits one prompt with `role: "test-planner"` and carries no `skipped_roles` key. So `--role test-planner` in that mode is simultaneously governed by property 4 (in the emitted set, therefore exit 0 with exactly one byte-identical entry) and by §4.2.1/property 5 (recognised nowhere, therefore exit 2). The release's headline flag has two contradictory specified outcomes for the one name §4.2 itself uses to motivate the emitted-set definition.
suggestion: Make recognition derive from the same set the match rule uses. Replace §4.2.1's three-source list with: exit 2 only when `<name>` is neither in the emitted set nor in `skipped_roles` nor in either phase's corpus — i.e. add the emitted set as a recognition source, so anything property 4 governs can never reach the exit-2 branch. State the ordering explicitly: property 4 is tried first, property 5 governs the remainder.

finding: Property 2 is measurably FALSE today, so a test written literally from it is red against a correct implementation. Property 2: "No prompt whose `output_path` is empty contains either clause. The modes that produce such a prompt are derived from what the code accepts — every `--perspective` value `review.go` validates, plus `--verify`." Measured on the current binary from the repository root: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective testing --test-path internal --spec-inline` emits one prompt, role `test-planner`, `output_path` == "" (41,293 chars), and its body CONTAINS §2.2's clause verbatim — because `--spec-inline` embeds this spec, and §2.2 quotes the clause in a fenced block. (Without `--spec-inline` the same invocation does not contain it: 32,885 chars, no match. `--spec-inline` is a shipped global flag on `tp review`, legal in every `--perspective` mode, and property 2 states no exclusion for it.) This is the exact hazard property 3, twelve lines below, records as measured-and-defeated after four drafts — "a 'the remainder contains neither clause string' form is forgeable by the document under review, since tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim" — reinstated in the property above it, and here it fires on the whole-spec embedding rather than the changed-section one, so it is live rather than latent.
suggestion: Property 2 states a containment predicate over a body the emitter does not control. Restate it as a property of the emitter, in the same shape property 1 already uses: 'No prompt whose `output_path` is empty ENDS WITH §2.3's construction.' That is decidable on any live emission, is not forgeable by any document the prompt embeds (an embedded spec is never the last 468 bytes), needs no `--spec-inline` exclusion, and is the negative of property 1 rather than a second, weaker kind of assertion.

finding: The exit-0/exit-2 split turns entirely on the word "recognises", which is defined by a three-element enumeration whose third element the spec never defines, and tp emits four names that fall on opposite sides depending on the reading. §4.2.1: "Only a name tp recognises nowhere — absent from the corpus for either phase, from `skipped_roles`, and from the built-ins — exits 2." "the built-ins" (plural) occurs exactly once in the document, at that line; the other four occurrences of "built-in" are singular and name only `regression`. Measured: `internal/cli/review.go` and `review_verify.go` emit four further non-corpus role names — `test-planner` (review.go:1532), `documentation-planner` (:1520), `code-auditor` (:1088) and `verifier` (review_verify.go:123). For `tp review <spec> --role verifier` in the default mode, engineer A reads "the built-ins" as {regression}, finds `verifier` in no corpus and no `skipped_roles`, and asserts exit 2; engineer B observes that tp plainly recognises the name (it emits it under `--verify`) and asserts exit 0 with `prompts: []`. Both readings are supported by the text and the two tests cannot both be green.
suggestion: Enumerate the set. Either write "the built-ins" as the literal set — `{regression}` — which makes the four mode-only role names exit 2 and is testable in one line; or define the recognition set as 'any `role` value this binary can emit in any mode', which makes them exit 0 and then requires §6.2.2 property 5 to say what the exit-0 payload carries when there is no `skipped_roles` entry to echo (see the companion finding at §6.2.2). Do not leave the choice to the implementer: it is the only thing that decides the exit code of a whole class of invocations.

finding: §4.2.3 names UnitKind.BriefCommand as the seam that appends --role <id>, but that function cannot see an id and it is not the only consumer, so the change is not buildable as written and the obvious implementation delivers nothing to a tp run unit. UnitKind.BriefCommand(t UnitTarget) is keyed on the kind and takes only the target (task file, spec); the unit id exists one level up, in newNextUnit(kind, id, target), which drops it before the call. An implementer must therefore invent the plumbing — widen the method, add an ID field to UnitTarget, or interpolate at the call site — and the spec names none of the three. The sharper half: engine.UnitPrompt(kind, t) calls the same id-less BriefCommand to build the {prompt} the runner hands the child, and that string is the only brief a tp run unit ever reads ('Run `tp review <spec>` first and follow the brief it returns'). Patching only the next_units[].brief_command path — which is the field §4.2.3 names and the only surface §6.2 property 10 asserts on — leaves every driver-spawned unit invoking the unrestricted command, so §4.3's 90.6% reaches no unit on the path §1 says pays §4's cost hardest. Observed live: this round's own units were spawned with exactly that id-less prompt.
suggestion: State how the unit id reaches the brief (BriefCommand gains the id, or UnitTarget carries it), and name engine.UnitPrompt as the second consumer that must render the same `--role <id>` string. Extend property 10 so it asserts on the prompt the driver hands the child, not only on next_units[].brief_command — otherwise the release's only measured benefit can pass its own property while never reaching a unit.

finding: Property 5's rewrite this round carves out `--perspective` and `--verify` as the modes where the `skipped_roles` echo has no source, and asserts that "in the default mode that role's reason is echoed from `skipped_roles`". That is still unsatisfiable in the default mode for the class §4.2.1's own recognition test creates: a name recognised because it is in the corpus for the *other* phase. §4.2.1 recognises a name "absent from the corpus for either phase" — so `tp review <spec> --role go-safety` (an audit corpus role) is recognised, must exit 0 with `prompts: []`, and must echo a reason. But `tp review` never considers audit roles, so it never produces a `skipped_roles` entry for one. Measured: this round's `tp review` payload carries `skipped_roles: []` and the `tp audit` payload carries `skipped_roles: []`; neither command lists the other phase's roles at all. The default-mode branch property 5 now claims as the working side of the split has no source for exactly the names §4.2.1 went out of its way to admit.
suggestion: Either narrow §4.2.1's recognition test to the *current phase's* corpus (making a cross-phase name an exit-2 unknown, with a hint saying it is the other phase's role), or give property 5 a third case: a name recognised only in the other phase's corpus exits 0 with `prompts: []` and a reason tp synthesises rather than echoes. Do not leave the phase qualifier in §4.2.1 while property 5 assumes a single-phase `skipped_roles`.

finding: This round repaired property 5's exit-0 branch by partitioning on MODE, but the branch's unsatisfiable case is a NAME class, and the repair does not reach it — so the branch is still unwritable in the very mode the new partition says it holds. Property 5 now reads: "A name tp recognises but the round does not emit exits 0 with `prompts: []`, and in the default mode that role's reason is echoed from `skipped_roles`", with the exemption granted to `--perspective` and `--verify` because those payloads carry no `skipped_roles` key. Measured: the DEFAULT-mode payload does carry `skipped_roles` (round 13 on this spec: present, length 0), but it carries an entry only for roles the panel derivation skipped. A name recognised solely because tp emits it in another mode — `verifier`, `test-planner`, `documentation-planner`, `code-auditor` — has no entry there in the default mode either. So under the reading that makes those names 'recognised' (see §4.2.1), property 5 requires a QA engineer to assert an echo of a reason that provably does not exist, in the default mode, which is the side of the partition the repair declared safe. The mode partition and the name partition are orthogonal and only the first has been drawn.
suggestion: After §4.2.1 fixes the recognition set, close property 5 over the cross product rather than over modes alone. If mode-only role names are OUT of the recognition set, say so in property 5 as well ('recognised' = in the corpus for either phase, or in this payload's `skipped_roles`, or `regression`), which makes the echo requirement total over the remaining names and the branch writable. If they are IN, property 5 needs a third case — recognised, not emitted, and no `skipped_roles` entry — with its own stated payload, or the echo clause has to be conditioned on the entry existing rather than on the mode.

finding: §2.3's emission predicate paragraph ends: "§4.4 records why the predicate is a property of the prompt rather than of the role." §4.4 records no such thing. Its two paragraphs are entirely about the regression prompt reaching four units and no unit, the driver defect in `BuildNextUnits`, Non-Goal 6, and property 11's set equality; the words predicate, `output_path` and role-versus-prompt do not appear. The justification the release's emission rule leans on points at a section that does not contain it — while the actual reason is available two subsections earlier (§2.2: "'the output file' is the antecedent the prompt already supplies", so a prompt with an empty `output_path` has no antecedent for either clause). This matters more than a normal broken reference because §6.2 property 2 was rewritten this round to *derive* the excluded mode set from code rather than list it, which leaves §2.3's citation as the only place a reader can look for why the predicate is shaped this way.
suggestion: Point the sentence at §2.2, or state the reason inline in §2.3: the predicate is a property of the prompt because both clauses reference "the output file this prompt names", which a prompt with an empty `output_path` does not name. Delete the §4.4 reference.

finding: Half the surface this release buys is `tp audit`, and §4 contains no audit measurement at all — every figure justifying `--role` is a `tp review` emission. §4.1's two tables (4 prompts / 41,015 B at round 3; 5 prompts / 131,727 B at round 4), the 90.6% never-read row, the '62% of the payload' regression share and §4.3's whole P1 paragraph ('a role unit receives 131,727 bytes to read 12,376') are all review payloads: they are derived from `buildReviewPrompts` and the auto-appended `regression` role. The cost side is then paid in full on both commands — `--role` registered on `tp audit` (§4.2.2's second table row), `UnitKind.BriefCommand` changed for `audit-role` as well as `review-role` (§4.2.3), property 1 'Holds for `tp review` and `tp audit`', property 6 'against each command's own flag set', property 7 'for both commands', and property 8, the release gate, inheriting that doubling across every spec in the repository. §6.1 records that the audit emissions are the more expensive of the two ('the `tp audit` half needs a working tree with git history because it detects affected files by `git diff`'). The review number also cannot be transferred by analogy, because its single largest term does not exist on the audit side: §4.1 and property 5 both establish that `regression` is `tp review`'s built-in, and it is 62% of the measured payload. Strip it and review's own waste falls from 90.6% to roughly (N−1)/N on a much smaller payload — which is what the audit half's real figure looks like, and the spec never states it. So the release's largest cost item is doubled on the strength of an unmeasured claim, in the section that exists to measure.
suggestion: Add one audit row to §4.1's second table — the audit panel size, payload bytes and per-unit read for one spec with an audit corpus — and scope §4.3's 90.6% explicitly to `tp review`, with the audit figure beside it. If the audit measurement is not worth taking, say so and state the bound the design implies ((N−1)/N of a payload with no `regression` term), so a reader can see that the audit half is justified by an argument rather than a measurement. Either way §7 should note that property 8 iterates two commands per spec, since that doubling is the release's biggest single cost and it is currently invisible in the section that gates on it.

finding: §4.2.2 states an evaluation-ordering guarantee whose only observable is a hint string the spec never pins, and §6.2's property for that behaviour asserts the exit code alone — which both orderings produce. §4.2.2: "The refusal is evaluated **before** the mode's own argument validation, so the hint an operator sees names the flag conflict rather than a missing `--findings`." Property 6, the property that implements it, says only: "`--role` is accepted in every mode that emits prompts and refused with exit 2 in every mode that emits none." Measured on the current binary, `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --verify` already exits 2 with `{"error":"--verify requires --findings","code":2}`, and `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --round 13 --verify` exits 2 with a different message again (`--verify is mutually exclusive with --round`) — so a wrongly ordered implementation exits 2 as well, and every assertion property 6 licenses is green either way. The one clause in §4.2 that only a test can protect is the one §6 does not test, and the hint text needed to test it is nowhere fixed (contrast §2.2 and §3.2, which are given verbatim for exactly this reason).
suggestion: Either give property 6 a second half — 'in a mode where `--role` is refused, the exit-2 error names `--role`, whatever else is also wrong with the invocation' — which is a substring assertion an engineer can write without pinning the whole string, and pair it with the one command that makes it discriminating (`tp review <spec> --merge --role <name>` with no `--output`, where the unordered implementation reports the merge-mode argument error instead); or drop the ordering sentence from §4.2.2 and let the hint be whichever error fires first, since an untested guarantee about message ordering is a claim the release cannot keep.

finding: Property 2, rewritten this round, derives the set of clause-free modes from code — "every `--perspective` value `review.go` validates, plus `--verify`" — instead of listing it. That derivation silently withholds §2's isolation constraint from an activity the spec itself says an agent performs: §4.2.3 quotes `review_loop.instruction` as directing the caller to "run an uncounted `--perspective regression` delta pass". Measured: `--perspective testing` emits its prompt with `output_path: ""`, so by §2.3's predicate and property 2 the delta-pass prompt carries neither clause. §2's motivating failure is a concurrent agent mutating the working tree and a second agent reporting the mutation as a defect — a delta-pass agent is exactly such an agent, and it is now specified to receive no isolation instruction. Nothing in §2.4, §4.4 or the Non-Goals records this exclusion as deliberate; before this round it was at least visible as a written mode list, and deriving it from code removes the last place a reader would notice it.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §2.4 or Non-Goal 4 stating that perspective and verify prompts are deliberately clause-free because they name no output file, and that the operator — not the prompt — carries the constraint for the delta pass. If that is not acceptable, give those prompts an `output_path` or emit §2.2's clause with an antecedent that does not depend on one.

finding: Property 4's payload rule — 'Every other top-level key is unchanged, and review_loop is unchanged except its instruction member' — is written entirely in tp review vocabulary, while §4.2 applies --role to tp audit as well, where the payload's shared keys are different and the rule produces a state the spec never contemplates. The audit payload carries top-level checklist (the flat list of every checklist item across all roles) and checklist_summary alongside prompts[], and each prompts[] entry separately carries its own checklist_items. Under `tp audit <spec> --role <name>` property 4 requires both top-level keys to stay whole, so the reduced payload enumerates the checklist items of roles for which it no longer emits a prompt. An implementer has to decide whether that is intended — reduce them to the selected role, or leave them and accept a checklist that disagrees with prompts[] — and no sentence in §4 or §6.2 rules on it. §4.2.2 was deliberately careful to enumerate the two commands' flag sets separately because 'the two commands do not have the same flag sets'; the payload rule was never given the same treatment, and the two commands do not have the same payload keys either.
suggestion: Give the payload rule the same per-command treatment §4.2.2 gives legality: say what --role does to a key that partitions by role but is emitted at top level, naming tp audit's checklist and checklist_summary explicitly — either 'reduced to the selected role's items' or 'unchanged, and the mismatch with prompts[] is accepted and why'. Property 4 currently states an exception mechanism (review_loop.instruction) for a key that exists on only one of the two commands it governs.

finding: Property 5's echo requirement has no observable that distinguishes a conforming implementation from one that does nothing, and the two readings produce contradictory assertions. §4.2.1 says the exit-0 case emits "the role's own entry present in `skipped_roles`"; property 5 says "that role's reason is echoed from `skipped_roles`". Measured: `skipped_roles` is a top-level key that the UNRESTRICTED payload already carries with that entry in it, and property 4's rule — "Every other top-level key is unchanged" — requires it to stay whole under `--role` for an emitted name. So for a non-emitted name, engineer A writes `assert payload['skipped_roles'] == [{'role': name, 'reason': r}]` (the flag filters, which is what 'echoed' implies and what makes the requirement mean anything), and engineer B writes `assert any(e['role'] == name for e in payload['skipped_roles'])` (the flag leaves the key alone, which is what 'present in' says and what property 4 requires elsewhere). One of the two is guaranteed red and nothing in §6.2 decides which. "present in" and "echoed" are not the same predicate.
suggestion: Pick one and write it as set equality or as membership, in both §4.2.1 and property 5, in the same words. If `--role` filters `skipped_roles` to the named role, say `skipped_roles` is exactly that one entry — and then state the exception in property 4, which currently forbids it. If it does not filter, drop 'echoed' for 'unchanged, and it contains that role's entry', so the assertion is membership and the property is honest that the exit code and the empty `prompts[]` are the whole observable.

finding: §6.3 states its own organising rule: the withdrawn constructions "are listed here rather than beside the properties they used to encumber, so that the properties stay readable and the reasons stay found." §6.2 does the opposite, and this round's edits widened the gap: property 3 (modified) now carries a five-line paragraph on four failed drafts; property 4 (modified) carries two sentences on a draft that opened as an unscoped universal and a successor that granted the exception at the wrong level; property 5 (modified) carries three separate draft post-mortems; property 9 is nothing but a withdrawal note. The §6.3 table meanwhile holds four rows, one of which (the cross-version baseline) duplicates the arc property 3 and property 9 already narrate in place. A section whose stated purpose is to keep draft history out of §6.2 sits below a §6.2 in which draft history is now the majority of the prose — and §6's own preamble names over-specification as the reason §6 "was the only section that never converged".
suggestion: Apply §6.3's rule to §6.2: move the four-draft arc from property 3, the two draft post-mortems from property 4 and the three from property 5 into §6.3's table as rows, and reduce each property to the assertion an implementation must satisfy. If a rationale must stay inline because the property is unreadable without it, amend §6.3's sentence to say so rather than stating a rule §6.2 does not follow.

finding: Property 3's rewrite this round leaves the document one cross-section magic number, and it is the one number this spec has already drifted on twice. Property 3 reads 'that same body with its last 468 bytes removed', and §1.1 defends the literal as necessary — '§6.2 property 3 fixes the suffix at 468 bytes, which is the figure an assertion can reach'. But property 1, in the same subsection, already requires an assertion that builds the suffix: 'ends with §2.3's construction exactly — trailing newline removed, then LF LF, §2.2's clause, LF LF, §3.2's clause, no trailing newline'. Any implementation of property 1 therefore holds the suffix string, and its length is free. 468 is not the figure an assertion can reach; it is the figure an assertion can derive and does not need to be told. That matters beyond tidiness because §1.1 spends ten lines on the history of this exact literal — an earlier draft called the suffix '467-byte', two further drafts minted and retired anti-drift devices for it, and §1.1 now declares the table the sole derivation. One literal outside the table keeps the drift surface open for the price of nothing: a future edit to §2.2's or §3.2's clause changes the suffix and leaves property 3 asserting a stale integer, silently, since a wrong strip length still produces a body that does not end with the suffix and the property passes.
suggestion: State property 3 without the number: 'an emitted body ends with property 1's suffix, and the body with that suffix removed does not itself end with it' — the strip length is len(suffix), from the same two clause strings property 1 already fixes. Then delete §1.1's sentence about 468 being 'the figure an assertion can reach' and keep only the table row that derives it, so the whole document contains the suffix length in exactly one place, which is what §1.1 says it wants.
